principles.why: Removing legislators’ control over their own district boundaries can reduce self-dealing; criteria must still protect equal population and legally required representation.
Public membership selection, criteria and hearings let voters examine how their districts were drawn.
Competitive entry and fair representation matter to residents whose votes are diluted by self-protecting maps.
Opponents can prefer line-drawing by directly accountable elected representatives to an appointed body; the legislature’s retained approval varies by state.
Some defend the existing elected-legislature constitutional arrangement.
A new commission entails selection, hearing and mapping administration; the direction depends on actual replacement costs, which are not quantified here.

principles.why: Supporters frame identity verification as protection against impersonation and harm to election integrity; this is their argument, not proof of prevalence or efficacy.
Supporters favor a common identity-verification standard. This support argument can coexist with unequal document access.
An intelligible verification rule can make administration auditable and improve claimed confidence.
Document requirements can burden eligible voters differently because possession and ability to obtain accepted ID differ.
Eligible voters without accepted documents must retain a realistic route to cast a counted ballot.
Opponents object to restricting an eligible citizen’s franchise for lack of documentation.
Free ID, voter education and cure/provisional processing add public administrative burdens. No cost size asserted.

principles.why: Agency registration reduces the extra step eligible people must navigate to enter the voter roll.
Automatic updates reduce registration-status discrepancies across eligible agency users. Coverage must include real citizenship/eligibility checks.
Shared agency-to-election data processing replaces repeated individual paper applications.
Accurate electronic rolls may reduce expensive provisional processing; implementation costs remain separate and unquantified.
Opponents resist government initiating registration without an individual application.
Consent, affiliation privacy and a usable opt-out matter, especially when notification comes after the agency transaction.
An obscure mailed opt-out can leave people unable to understand or decline the action.

principles.why: Regular turnover limits an individual officeholder’s accumulated control over public power.
Open seats make room for challengers who otherwise face entrenched incumbents.
Supporters seek a closer connection between officeholders and ordinary constituents rather than a permanent governing class.
A binding limit removes the voter’s option to reelect the otherwise eligible experienced representative they prefer.
Opponents value continuity and established legislative experience rather than forced rotation.
Losing experienced members can make sustaining complex public administration harder; this is an authored institutional argument, not a quantified performance finding.

principles.why: Cooling-off rules address the revolving-door relationship between official decisions and later paid representation. A waiting period does not by itself publish lobbying contacts.
Supporters object to privileged access obtained from recent public office rather than equal access for ordinary petitioners.
Separating public office from immediately monetized influence constrains personal use of state power.
A broad ban restricts paid speech, petition and post-office occupations; Missouri’s constitutional rejection demonstrates these are real legal interests.
Former officials may resist a blanket restriction on lawful work beyond narrowly defined conflicts. Paid/unpaid exceptions matter.
A broad rule can bar useful public-agency representation; existing public-employer exemptions identify that trade-off.

principles.why: Local democratic bodies can respond to conditions and preferences of people who live with the decision.
Local reform can meet unmet needs when statewide action is unavailable, subject to rights and legal limits.
Effective local fiscal and regulatory authority supports services residents choose together.
Nearby decision makers and local civic participation can improve public accountability.
Statewide interests include equal legal protections and rules that should not change arbitrarily across municipal borders.
Opponents may resist additional local regulatory power over private activity. Home rule is authority, not a mandate to regulate.
Cross-border spillovers and administrative duplication can justify statewide coordination; no dollar amount is inferred.
